title: The iconostasis
hook: the Orthodox icon screen, both veil and window

segments.voice: Yesterday, the basilica: an old Roman hall turned into a church, a long nave leading up to a rounded apse. Your line was the long walk. What were you walking toward yesterday? Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

At the far end of an Orthodox church, right where the long walk would reach the altar, there's a wall. Not plain stone. A wall of faces. Christ on one side of a central doorway. On the other, Mary, holding him as a child. Angels painted on the side doors. Saints in rows, gold behind every head. Candles flicker in front of them, and in that light the faces seem to shift. A small child near the front stares straight up. Then, at a certain moment in the service, the central doors swing open, and through the gap there's the altar, and light, and a priest moving. A little later, the doors close again. Today: the iconostasis.

The iconostasis is the screen of icons standing between the nave, where the people are, and the sanctuary, where the altar is. Orthodox Christians describe it two ways at once. First, a veil. In the temple in Jerusalem, a veil hung before the holiest place. Matthew's Gospel says that when Jesus died, "behold, the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom." So the screen still marks a threshold. Something holy is behind it, and it isn't simply put on display. Second, a window. In the Orthodox understanding an icon is not decoration. Paul's letter to the Colossians calls Christ "the image of the invisible God," and the Greek word there for image is eikon. Orthodox Christians teach that because God became visible in Christ, his face may be painted, and an icon opens onto the one it shows. So standing before the screen, the congregation isn't facing a wall. It's facing a crowd: Christ, Mary, the saints, looking back. Third, the doors. The central ones, called the royal or holy doors, open and close during the liturgy. The gospel book passes through them. At communion, the cup is brought out through them. Hidden, then shown, then hidden. Paul put that same rhythm into one sentence: "For now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face." Other churches arrange this space in other ways, some with the altar standing in full view. The Orthodox screen holds both halves of Paul's line in one wall.
screen: `A WINDOW: THE IMAGE OF THE INVISIBLE GOD.`
`THROUGH A GLASS, DARKLY; THEN FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look at an icon screen. If you can, find a photo of one, or step into an Orthodox church some day and stand before the real thing. For now, settle, and breathe. Let your eyes rest on a single face, and stay there. Notice the doors in the middle, closed for now. You don't have to know what's behind them. If you pray, you can say Paul's words quietly: now we see through a glass, darkly; but then face to face. Or simply let the face look back at you while you breathe. The bell holds the time.
screen: `NOW WE SEE THROUGH A GLASS, DARKLY; BUT THEN FACE TO FACE.`

segments.voice: The iconostasis. The screen of icons between the people and the altar in an Orthodox church: a veil that hides, and a window of faces that shows.

Your line: veil and window. Today, notice one thing that both hides and shows: a curtain with light around its edges, a door left half open, a face keeping something back. Day one thousand three hundred fifty-two.

howItsDone: In Orthodox churches an iconostasis stands between the nave and the altar; worshipers light candles before its icons and venerate them, and the central doors open and close at set moments of the Divine Liturgy.

fork.setup: you're standing before an icon screen, and the central doors are closed. what is the screen doing?
options: hiding and showing at the same time
fork.reveal: Orthodox Christians call it both veil and window: it marks off the altar, and its faces look straight back at you.

original.note: Greek: image. The word in Colossians 1:15, "the image of the invisible God."

trapdoor: what you thought: a wall of paintings that blocks the view.
what it means: the screen between people and altar, a veil and a window at once.
what a scholar hears: Colossians calls Christ the eikon of the invisible God, the ground Orthodox Christians give for painting his face at all.

notes: Review picks up day 1351 from the index (its script was not on disk when this was written).
Hook places Christ on one side of the central doors and Mary holding the child on the other, angels on the side doors; confirm this is a fair general description without claiming a fixed rule.
Greek of Colossians 1:15 has eikon (εἰκών) for 'image'; confirm. No etymology of 'iconostasis' is claimed.
'Royal or holy doors' and what passes through them (gospel book, bread and cup): an Orthodox Keeper should confirm wording.
The Orthodox theology of icons (because God became visible in Christ, he may be painted) is stated as Orthodox teaching; confirm phrasing.
Editor: cut the Hebrews 10:20 veil quotation (same passage as day 1351's teach) and its source entry.

Audit (2026-10-02): at the Little and Great Entrances the procession goes out by the north door and in through the royal doors, so 'the gospel book is carried out through them' was inaccurate; now 'passes through them', and communion's cup 'brought out through them'.
